title: IS ONAN REALLY A BIBLE STORY ABOUT MASTURBATION? Read What He Was Actually Doing
paragraphs: IS ONAN REALLY A BIBLE STORY ABOUT MASTURBATION? Read What He Was Actually Doing

Genesis 38 has been quoted for generations as though Onan’s sin were obvious. But read the Hebrew carefully, follow the story all the way to Tamar, Judah, Perez—and eventually Jesus Christ—and you may discover that this disturbing chapter is confronting something far deeper than the explanation many Christians were given.
There are Bible stories we think we know because somebody explained them to us before we ever slowed down long enough to read them.
Onan is one of them.
Maybe you heard his name in a sermon about sexual sin.
Maybe someone told you, “God killed Onan because he spilled his seed.”
Maybe Genesis 38 was used as a quick answer to a question about masturbation, and because the story is uncomfortable, nobody stayed in the chapter long enough to ask the most important question:
What does the Bible actually say Onan was doing—and why does the text say he did it?
That question matters.
Not because sexual holiness does not matter.
It does.

Jesus takes sexual purity so seriously that He moves the conversation beyond outward behavior and into the desires of the heart. Christ does not give us permission to make peace with lust simply because we discover that a particular proof text has been misunderstood.
But biblical holiness must be built on biblical truth.
We should never have to make Scripture say something it does not say in order to defend something Scripture genuinely teaches.
And Genesis 38 deserves to be heard on its own terms.
The story begins in a broken family.
Judah, one of Jacob’s sons, has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Judah obtains a wife named Tamar for his firstborn, Er.
Then Genesis gives us a terrifyingly brief sentence.
Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
Tamar is now a childless widow.
And this is where Onan enters the story.
Judah tells him:
“בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ”
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehakem zera le’achikha.
In context:
“Go in to your brother’s wife, perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
That word וְיַבֵּם — veyabbem is crucial.

It refers to performing the duty of a brother-in-law toward the widow. The social and family institution reflected here is what is commonly called levirate marriage, from the Latin levir, meaning “husband’s brother.”

The practice would later appear explicitly in Israel’s law in Deuteronomy 25:5–10. Genesis 38 occurs much earlier in the biblical storyline, but the family obligation behind the episode is unmistakable.
Tamar had lost her husband.
She had no child through whom her dead husband’s family line could continue.
Onan was commanded to fulfill his obligation toward her and to raise offspring for his brother.
And then Scripture tells us exactly what was happening inside Onan.
This is the sentence people sometimes rush past:
“וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע”
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
Stop there.
The narrator has just given us Onan’s motive.
He knew.
That matters enormously.
The story is not describing an unexplained bodily act and leaving us to guess why God was angry.
It tells us what Onan knew.
Then it tells us what he did.
Then it tells us why he did it.
Genesis 38:9 continues:
“וְהָיָה אִם־בָּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו”
The wording describes Onan going in to his brother’s wife and then ruining, wasting, or spilling on the ground so that he would not give offspring to his brother.
Those final words are devastating:
לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו
levilti netan-zera le’achiv
“so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
The Bible tells us his purpose.
Onan was not alone in a private act of masturbation.
He was having sexual relations with Tamar while deliberately preventing the sexual union from accomplishing the very family obligation for which he had gone to her.
In modern terminology, the physical action described is much closer to withdrawal or coitus interruptus than masturbation.
But even saying only that does not yet reach the moral center of the story.
Because Genesis is interested in more than the mechanics.
Onan wanted the sexual relationship while deliberately withholding what his responsibility to Tamar and his deceased brother required.
He took.
He refused to give.
He entered Tamar’s body while intentionally frustrating the obligation attached to that relationship.
And apparently this was not an accidental, one-time event.
The Hebrew construction is commonly understood as describing what happened when he went in to her—an ongoing pattern represented in many translations by language such as “whenever.”
Imagine Tamar inside this story.
She has already buried her husband.
Her future is insecure.
Her place in the family is fragile.
Now another man enters her life under an obligation connected with providing offspring for the deceased brother.
But Onan knows the child would not be reckoned as his in the relevant sense.
So he repeatedly takes what he wants while ensuring Tamar does not conceive.
That changes how the scene feels.
This is not merely a story about semen touching the ground.

It is a story involving selfishness, family obligation, sexuality, inheritance, deception, and a vulnerable widow whose future is being controlled by men who are not faithfully fulfilling their responsibilities toward her.
Onan appears to want the benefits without accepting the cost.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Intimacy without faithfulness to the purpose for which he had been given Tamar.
And suddenly Genesis 38 stops feeling ancient.
Because that temptation is still alive.
We want blessing without surrender.
Sex without covenant.
Grace without repentance.
Jesus without lordship.
Forgiveness without confession.
Christian identity without carrying a cross.
We want enough of God to soothe our conscience but sometimes not enough of God to interfere with what we secretly refuse to surrender.
Onan’s story is uncomfortable because somewhere beneath its ancient customs is an intensely modern human impulse:
How much can I take while giving as little of myself as possible?
Then comes Genesis 38:10.
“וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה”
Vayyera be’enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the sight of the LORD.”
Notice the emphasis.
What he did was evil.
We should be careful here.

Genesis 38 certainly concerns sexual behavior, but it does not identify Onan’s act as masturbation. The immediate narrative explicitly connects his behavior to intercourse with Tamar and his deliberate determination not to provide offspring for his brother.
That does not mean Christians should therefore conclude, “So anything involving masturbation, pornography, fantasy, or lust must be morally harmless.”
That conclusion would make the same interpretive mistake in the opposite direction.
Genesis 38 should not be forced to answer a question it is not directly addressing.

The Christian evaluation of masturbation has to be considered within the Bible’s broader teaching about lust, self-control, holiness, the body, marriage, conscience, love of neighbor, and whether our desires are mastering us rather than being brought under the lordship of Christ.
Pornography, for example, introduces additional moral realities involving lust, objectification, exploitation, and the cultivation of desires toward people who are being consumed as objects.
Jesus’ teaching about lust in Matthew 5:27–30 cannot simply be erased because Genesis 38 has sometimes been misused.
But neither should Genesis 38 be rewritten to say “masturbation” when that is not what the narrative actually describes.
Truth does not need a manipulated Bible verse to defend it.
And there is something even larger happening in Genesis 38.
Onan dies.
Judah still has another son, Shelah.
Tamar is told to remain a widow until Shelah grows up.
But time passes.
And the promise is not fulfilled.
Tamar realizes she has not been given to Shelah.
Then the story becomes one of the strangest scandals in Genesis.
Tamar disguises herself.
Judah does not recognize her.
He sleeps with her.
She becomes pregnant.
Later, when Judah hears that Tamar is pregnant, his response is ferocious.
He is prepared to condemn her.
Until Tamar produces the identifying items Judah himself had given her.
The trap closes.
The man ready to expose someone else’s sexual scandal suddenly discovers himself standing inside it.
And then Judah says words that crack the story open:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
And Judah explains why:
Because he had not given Tamar to his son Shelah.
There it is again.
Responsibility.
Failure.
Exposure.
A man who could see another person’s apparent sin suddenly had to confront his own.
Have you ever done that?
Seen somebody else’s failure immediately while becoming strangely blind around your own?
Condemned somebody for the visible wreckage of their life while carefully hiding the private compromises in yours?
Judah’s story is not comfortable because grace rarely begins by flattering us.
Sometimes God loves us enough to let the evidence land on the table.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
The browser history.
The secret conversation.
The hidden resentment.
The private habit.
The money nobody knows about.
The bitterness dressed up as discernment.
The religious performance covering a starving soul.
The thing we hoped would remain buried.
And then comes the moment every sinner eventually needs:
Not merely, “Look what they did.”
But—
Lord, look what I have become.
Yet Genesis 38 does not end with exposure.
Tamar gives birth to twins.
One is named Perez.
And if you know the rest of the Bible, that name should stop you.
Because generations later, the opening chapter of Matthew deliberately includes this scandalous family history in the genealogy of Jesus Christ:
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
Perez.
The child born from this shattered chapter becomes part of the genealogical line through which Matthew traces the ancestry of Jesus the Messiah.
Think about that.
Genesis 38 contains death.
Sexual wrongdoing.
Self-interest.
Broken promises.
Deception.
Hypocrisy.
Public shame.
Family dysfunction.
And consequences that cannot simply be erased.
If human beings were writing a polished résumé for the Messiah, this is the kind of chapter we might quietly delete.
God did not.
Tamar is named.
Judah is named.
Perez is named.
The scandal remains visible.
And Christ enters the human story through a family line in which grace does not pretend the wreckage never happened.
That is not God approving evil.
It is God demonstrating that human sin cannot outmaneuver His redemptive purposes.
This is where Genesis 38 becomes more than a debate about Onan.
Because perhaps you clicked this article expecting an answer about masturbation.
And perhaps somewhere along the way Scripture started answering a question you were not expecting to ask.
What are you doing with the things nobody knows about?
Maybe your struggle is sexual.
Maybe pornography has become the room you enter whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
Maybe masturbation has become intertwined with fantasies you know are reshaping the way you see people.
Maybe you keep promising Jesus, “This is the last time.”
Then night comes.
The temptation comes.
The screen lights up.
And afterward there is silence.
Shame.
Prayer.
Promises.
Failure.
Repeat.
Or maybe your hidden place has nothing to do with sexuality.
Maybe it is greed.
An affair.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
A double life.
Alcohol.
Envy.
Dishonesty.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Or maybe you have become frighteningly good at looking spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not an invitation to rename darkness as light.
And it is not an invitation to hide from God until you have repaired yourself.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People with chapters they wish could be torn out of the book.
The answer to shame is not pretending sin is harmless.
The answer is bringing sin into the light and running toward the Savior who bore sin at the cross.
Christ did not die so we could become more sophisticated at hiding.
He died to redeem us.
At Calvary, Jesus carried guilt He did not commit for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
And He rose again.
That means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance is not God standing over you saying, “Make yourself worthy and perhaps I will love you again.”
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy you could never purchase.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment—and His mercy is so great that the repentant sinner can be forgiven, cleansed, restored, and transformed.
So if Genesis 38 has been used to terrify you with something the passage itself does not actually say, read it again.
But if discovering the context makes you want to use biblical accuracy as permission to protect a hidden lust, read your own heart again too.
Do not exchange one distortion for another.
The question is bigger than:
“Can I technically prove this particular behavior is forbidden by Onan’s story?”
A follower of Jesus eventually has to ask:
Is this drawing me toward Christ or training my heart away from Him?
Is it feeding lust?
Is it controlling me?
Is another human being becoming an object in my imagination?
Can I bring this before Jesus without hiding?
Am I walking in self-control?
Am I seeking holiness—or merely searching for the nearest loophole?
Because loopholes have never transformed anyone into the likeness of Christ.
Jesus does.
And if something hidden has been exposed in you while reading this, do not disappear into shame.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Put practical boundaries around the places where you repeatedly fall.
Speak to a mature, trustworthy Christian who will walk with you without turning your confession into gossip.
And keep returning to Christ.
If you fall, do not turn failure into permission to surrender completely.
Get up.
Return.
Confess again.
Fight again.
Not because your fighting purchases the love of God, but because belonging to Christ means sin no longer gets to sit unquestioned on the throne.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Not because every sentence is easy.
There may be someone among your friends who has carried unnecessary condemnation for years because nobody ever showed them what Genesis 38 actually says.
There may also be someone using biblical misunderstanding as an excuse to stop pursuing holiness.
Both people need truth.
Send this privately to the person who has been afraid to tell anybody that they are struggling.
Christian generosity is to be willing, sincere, and directed according to conscience before God.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel Warrior continue producing and sharing Christ-centered resources with people who need them. Supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not to buy God’s approval.
But because Gospel work requires people willing to pray, share, serve, give, and stand behind it.
Send it to someone who needs it.
Because Onan’s story was never meant to become a convenient slogan detached from its context.
It is darker than that.
More human than that.
And when Genesis 38 is allowed to finish telling its story, it points beyond Onan.
Beyond Tamar.
Beyond Judah.
Beyond Perez.
Down through generations of broken human beings until Matthew opens his Gospel and begins tracing a family line toward one Name.
Jesus.
The Savior who was not ashamed to enter a human family tree scarred by scandal.
The King who came near to sinners.
The Lamb who carried our guilt.
The risen Christ who still calls people out of hiding.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
Your sin may require real repentance.
Your choices may carry real consequences.
But for the person who turns to Jesus Christ, the scandal does not get the final sentence.
The chapter you are most ashamed for Jesus to read may become the very place where you finally discover how deeply you needed His grace.
